questions.stem: In the 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 (reward $-1$ per move, $\gamma = 1$) the equiprobable random policy has $v_\pi(11) = -14$ and terminal value 0. Moving down from state 11 reaches the terminal state; moving down from state 7 reaches state 11. Find $q_\pi(11, \text{down})$ and $q_\pi(7, \text{down})$.
solution: For a deterministic move, $q_\pi(s, a) = r + \gamma v_\pi(s')$.
$q_\pi(11, \text{down}) = -1 + 1 \cdot v_\pi(\text{terminal}) = -1 + 0 = -1$.
questions.explanation: An action value is one step of reward plus the value of the state you land in. After that step the policy π takes over.

misconceptions.why: That is v_π(11), the average over all four actions. Choosing down terminates immediately.

questions.stem: Run two-array iterative policy evaluation (4.5) on the 4×4 gridworld from $v_0 = 0$. After one sweep every nonterminal state has $v_1 = -1$. Compute the exact values $v_2(1)$ and $v_2(6)$. State 1 neighbours the terminal state on its left; state 6 has nonterminal neighbours 2, 5, 7 and 10.
solution: $v_2(s) = -1 + \tfrac14 \sum_{\text{4 moves}} v_1(s')$.
State 1: the moves lead to the terminal state (0), state 1 itself (up, off the grid: $-1$), state 2 ($-1$) and state 5 ($-1$). So $v_2(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 3) = -1.75$.
State 6: all four successors have $v_1 = -1$, so $v_2(6) = -1 + \tfrac14(-4) = -2$.
questions.explanation: Figure 4.2 prints $v_2(1)$ as −1.7. The exact value is −1.75 (see the figure-rounding flag on Example 4.1).

misconceptions.why: That is the printed one-decimal value. The exact two-array iterate is −1.75.

questions.stem: Put the steps of one pass of in-place iterative policy evaluation (Figure 4.1) in order.
options: Set $\Delta \leftarrow 0$
For the next state $s$, remember $v \leftarrow V(s)$
Replace $V(s)$ by its full backup $\sum_a \pi(a|s)\sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]$
Update $\Delta \leftarrow \max(\Delta, |v - V(s)|)$
After all states, stop if $\Delta < \theta$; otherwise start another sweep
solution: Reset the largest-change tracker at the start of each sweep.
For each state: save the old value, back it up in place, record the change.
Test the stopping condition once the sweep is complete.
questions.explanation: The old value must be saved before the backup overwrites it, or the change Δ cannot be measured.

questions.stem: In the 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 (equiprobable random policy, reward $-1$ per move, $\gamma = 1$), $v_\pi(12) = -22$, $v_\pi(13) = -20$ and $v_\pi(14) = -14$. A new state 15 is added below state 13. From 15, the moves left, up, right and down lead to 12, 13, 14 and 15. (i) If all the original transitions are unchanged, what is $v_\pi(15)$? (ii) If, in addition, moving down from 13 now leads to 15, what is $v_\pi(15)$?
solution: (i) No original state can reach 15, so their values stay as in Figure 4.2. The Bellman equation at 15: $v = -1 + \tfrac14(-22 - 20 - 14 + v)$.

(ii) Now 13's down move leads to 15 instead of back to 13. Try the values from (i): 13's equation used to contain $v(13) = -20$ for its down move, and now contains $v(15) = -20$. These are the same number, so every equation still holds.
$v_\pi$ is the unique solution of its Bellman equations, so the values are unchanged and $v_\pi(15) = -20$ again.
questions.explanation: This is Exercise 4.2 of the draft, reworded. The app solves both versions of the extended gridworld numerically (check ch04-q004). The second part works because state 15 turns out to have exactly the value of state 13.

misconceptions.why: The change only swaps one successor value $-20$ for another $-20$, so the solution of the equations does not move.

questions.stem: Continue two-array iterative policy evaluation (4.5) on the 4×4 gridworld. From $v_2$, where states 1, 4, 11 and 14 have $-1.75$ and every other nonterminal state has $-2$, compute the exact values $v_3(1)$ and $v_3(5)$. State 5's neighbours are 1 (up), 9 (down), 6 (right) and 4 (left).
solution: $v_3(s) = -1 + \tfrac14 \sum_{\text{4 moves}} v_2(s')$.
State 1: the moves lead to the terminal state (0), state 1 itself (up, off the grid: $-1.75$), state 2 ($-2$) and state 5 ($-2$). So $v_3(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(-5.75) = -2.4375$.
questions.explanation: Figure 4.2 prints these values as $-2.4$ and $-2.9$. Under ordinary rounding, $-2.875$ to one decimal would also be $-2.9$, and $-2.4375$ would be $-2.4$ (see the figure-rounding flag on Example 4.1).

questions.stem: How does the in-place version of iterative policy evaluation (Figure 4.1) differ from the two-array version of (4.5)?
options: Each backed-up value immediately replaces the old one, so later backups in the same sweep may use new values; it also converges to $v_\pi$, usually faster
Only the two-array version converges to $v_\pi$
The in-place version needs one array for old values and one for new values
In the in-place version the order in which states are backed up makes no difference to the speed of convergence
optionNotes: Correct, as §4.1 describes. The app also checks that both versions reach the same $v_\pi$ (check ch04.in-place-converges-to-same-v).
The draft states that the in-place algorithm also converges to $v_\pi$.
It is the two-array version that keeps separate arrays for $v_k$ and $v_{k+1}$.
The draft says the sweep order strongly affects how quickly the in-place version converges.
solution: Two-array: compute all of $v_{k+1}$ from $v_k$, leaving $v_k$ untouched.
In-place: one array, where each backup overwrites its state's value, so later backups can use values already updated in this sweep.
Both converge to $v_\pi$. The in-place version usually converges faster, and its speed depends on the order of the sweep.
questions.explanation: The draft usually has the in-place version in mind when it discusses DP algorithms.

questions.stem: True or false: in general, iterative policy evaluation reaches $v_\pi$ exactly after a finite number of sweeps.
solution: The sequence $\{v_k\}$ converges to $v_\pi$ as $k \to \infty$: it is a limit.
In practice the algorithm is stopped once the largest change in a sweep falls below a small threshold $\theta$, leaving $V \approx v_\pi$.
questions.explanation: This is why Figure 4.1 outputs $V \approx v_\pi$ rather than $v_\pi$.

questions.stem: In Figure 4.1, $\Delta$ is set to 0 at the start of each sweep, and each backup does $\Delta \leftarrow \max(\Delta, |v - V(s)|)$. What does $\Delta$ hold when the test $\Delta < \theta$ is made?
options: The largest change made to any single state's value during the sweep just completed
The error $|V(s) - v_\pi(s)|$ at the last state backed up
The total change summed over all states in the sweep
The change made to the last state backed up
optionNotes: Correct: $\Delta$ is reset each sweep and takes the maximum over every backup in it.
$v_\pi$ is unknown, which is why it is being computed. $\Delta$ measures how much the values changed, not their distance from $v_\pi$.
The update takes a maximum, not a sum.
$\Delta$ keeps the largest change seen anywhere in the sweep, not only the last one.
solution: At the start of a sweep $\Delta = 0$.
After each state's backup, $\Delta$ becomes the larger of itself and that state's change $|v - V(s)|$.
At the end of the sweep $\Delta = \max_s |\text{change at } s|$. This is the stopping test the draft describes.
questions.explanation: A small $\Delta$ means the values have nearly stopped changing. It is a practical stopping rule, not a certificate of exact equality with $v_\pi$.

verification.note: Figure 4.1 and the stopping rule, printed p. 92.

questions.stem: Run two-array value iteration (4.10) on the 4×4 gridworld (γ = 1) from $v_0 = 0$. After one sweep every nonterminal state has $v_1 = -1$. Compute $v_2(1)$ and $v_2(6)$.
solution: $v_2(s) = \max_a [-1 + v_1(s')]$, with $v_1 = 0$ at the terminal states and $-1$ elsewhere.
State 1 can move left into the terminal state: $v_2(1) = -1 + 0 = -1$.
State 6 has only nonterminal neighbours: $v_2(6) = -1 + (-1) = -2$.
questions.explanation: Compare $v_2(1) = -1.75$ under policy evaluation of the random policy: the max picks the best move instead of averaging over all four.

misconceptions.why: That is the policy-evaluation value, which averages over the random policy's moves. Value iteration takes the maximum.

questions.stem: Solve the gambler's problem (Example 4.3) with $p_h = 0.4$ by value iteration. What are $v_*(25)$ and $v_*(50)$, the optimal probabilities of reaching a capital of 100 from capital 25 and from capital 50?
solution: From capital 50, staking everything wins with probability $p_h = 0.4$, and no strategy does better when $p_h < \tfrac12$.
From capital 25, staking 25 reaches capital 50 with probability 0.4, and from there the best is 0.4 again: $v_*(25) = 0.4 \cdot 0.4 = 0.16$.
Value iteration converges to these values (Figure 4.6).
questions.explanation: With an unfavourable coin, bold play maximises the chance of reaching the goal, so these are the values of bold play.

questions.stem: Why does policy iteration on a finite MDP reach an optimal policy after finitely many iterations?
options: There are finitely many deterministic policies, and each improvement is strict unless the policy is already optimal
Each policy evaluation is exact after one sweep
The discount factor γ < 1 forces the values to shrink each iteration
The value function changes by less than θ after each improvement
optionNotes: Correct: strict improvement plus a finite set of policies means the process cannot go on for ever.
Evaluation is itself iterative and usually needs many sweeps.
The argument does not depend on γ < 1; the gridworld example uses γ = 1.
θ controls when an evaluation stops, not how many improvements are needed.
solution: Each improvement step gives a strictly better policy unless the current one is already optimal (the policy improvement theorem).
A finite MDP has only finitely many deterministic policies, so no policy can repeat and the sequence must end at an optimal one.
questions.explanation: The draft gives this argument on p. 97. The Figure 4.3 pseudocode can still cycle between equally good policies, which the draft acknowledges.

verification.note: The finite-convergence argument, printed p. 97, checked against the text layer.

questions.stem: Run policy iteration on the 4×4 gridworld (γ = 1), starting from the equiprobable random policy. After the first improvement the policy is greedy with respect to $v_{\text{random}}$. What are $v_{\pi_1}(1)$ and $v_{\pi_1}(6)$ for that improved policy? State 1 is next to the top-left terminal corner; state 6 is in row 1, column 2.
solution: $v_{\text{random}}$ (Figure 4.2) increases towards the two terminal corners, so the greedy policy moves each state along a shortest path to a corner.
Every move costs −1, so $v_{\pi_1}(s)$ is minus the number of moves to the nearer corner.
State 1 is one move from the corner: $v_{\pi_1}(1) = -1$. State 6 is three moves from either corner: $v_{\pi_1}(6) = -3$.
questions.explanation: On this problem one improvement already gives an optimal policy, as the draft notes for Figure 4.2.

questions.stem: In Jack's car rental, the first location starts a day with 2 cars available, and rental requests there are Poisson with mean 3. Since a request with no car available is lost, the number rented is $\min(\text{requests}, 2)$. What is the expected number of cars rented, and the expected credit at $10 per rental?
solution: Credit: $10 \times 1.7511 \approx \$17.51$.
questions.explanation: Cars that are not available cannot be rented, so the expected reward is capped by the stock: this is why moving cars pays.

misconceptions.why: Only 2 cars are available; requests beyond that are lost.

questions.stem: Jack's car rental keeps between 0 and 20 cars at each of two locations, and each night moves a net number of cars between them, at most 5 in either direction. How many states does the MDP have, and how many actions are available in a state with plenty of cars at both locations?
solution: States: $21 \times 21 = 441$ pairs (cars at each location, 0 to 20).
Actions: net moves $-5, \ldots, 5$, that is 11 (fewer when a location has fewer than 5 cars).
questions.explanation: Small enough for exact DP, large enough that the optimal policy is not obvious.

questions.stem: The 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 has 14 nonterminal states with 4 actions each. How many deterministic policies does it have? (Policy iteration finds an optimal one after a single improvement.)
solution: One action per state, chosen independently: $m^n = 4^{14} = 268{,}435{,}456$.
questions.explanation: Direct search through m^n policies is hopeless even here; DP is polynomial in n and m.

questions.stem: Solve the gambler's problem with a heads probability of $p_h = 0.25$ by value iteration (the dynamic programming laboratory can do it). What are $v_*(25)$ and $v_*(50)$?
solution: With an unfavourable coin, bold play is optimal: from 50, stake everything: $v_*(50) = p_h = 0.25$.
From 25, stake 25 to reach 50, then stake 50: $v_*(25) = p_h^2 = 0.0625$.
questions.explanation: With p_h < 0.5 every flip loses money on average, so the fewer flips the better.

questions.stem: Backgammon has about $10^{20}$ states. If value-iteration backups could be done at a million states per second, how many years would one full sweep take (365.25-day years)?
solution: $10^{14} / (365.25 \times 24 \times 3600) \approx 3.17 \times 10^6$ years.
questions.explanation: The draft's 'over a thousand years' is true, and an understatement: sweeps are out of the question, which is why asynchronous DP matters.

questions.stem: Give the equations for action values that correspond to (4.3), (4.4) and (4.5): the definition of $q_\pi$ as a one-step expectation, its Bellman equation written with $p(s', r|s, a)$, and the update that computes successive approximations $q_0, q_1, q_2, \ldots$
questions.answer: $q_\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma q_\pi(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = a]$; $q_\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a'|s') q_\pi(s', a')\big]$; $q_{k+1}(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a'|s') q_k(s', a')\big]$ for all $s, a$.
solution: Start from q_π(s, a) = E_π[G_t | S_t = s, A_t = a] and split off the first reward.
The next action A_{t+1} is drawn from π, so average q_π(s′, ·) with π(·|s′).
Turn the equation into an assignment with q_k on the right.
questions.explanation: Iterating this update converges to q_π, just as (4.5) converges to v_π.

rubric.point: Analogue of (4.3): expectation of R_{t+1} + γ q_π(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) given S_t = s, A_t = a
Analogue of (4.4): sum over s′, r of p(s′, r|s, a), with the next action averaged under π
Analogue of (4.5): q_{k+1} on the left, q_k on the right, for all state–action pairs
Notes that the first action is given (no π for it)

verification.note: Exercise 4.3, printed p. 110; the iteration is checked to converge to q_π on the 5×5 gridworld.

questions.stem: In an undiscounted episodic task, a policy may never reach the terminal state (for example, it moves back and forth between two cells of the gridworld), so $v_\pi(s)$ can be $-\infty$ and the algorithm of Figure 4.1 never stops. As a practical matter, how could the algorithm be changed so that it always terminates? Assume that the optimal policy does terminate.
questions.answer: Any of: cap the number of sweeps and stop with a warning; detect divergence (values falling below a bound such as −(maximum possible episode cost) or growing without limit) and report $-\infty$ for those states; add a small discount (γ slightly below 1) so every value is finite; or, inside policy iteration, start from a policy known to terminate, so that every policy produced by improvement is at least as good and therefore also terminates. The last is the principled fix: improvement never makes values worse, so it can never produce a non-terminating policy from a terminating one.
solution: Ask what makes Δ never fall below θ: values that keep decreasing.
Either bound the computation, change the problem slightly (discount), or avoid evaluating such policies at all.
questions.explanation: The dynamic programming laboratory handles the same issue by reporting an evaluation that does not converge.

rubric.point: Proposes a stopping safeguard: a sweep limit, or a bound that detects values diverging
Or proposes discounting or a per-step cap so that values stay finite
Notes the policy-iteration route: start from a terminating policy; improvement keeps every later policy terminating

questions.stem: Define policy iteration for action values: write a complete algorithm that computes $q_*$, in the style of Figure 4.3 (which computes $v_*$). The draft stresses that the ideas in this exercise are used throughout the rest of the book.
questions.answer: 1. Initialise $Q(s, a)$ arbitrarily and a deterministic $\pi(s) \in \mathcal{A}(s)$ for all s. 2. Policy evaluation: repeat, with $\Delta \leftarrow 0$: for each $(s, a)$: $q \leftarrow Q(s, a)$; $Q(s, a) \leftarrow \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)[r + \gamma Q(s', \pi(s'))]$; $\Delta \leftarrow \max(\Delta, |q - Q(s, a)|)$; until $\Delta < \theta$. 3. Policy improvement: stable ← true; for each s: $a \leftarrow \pi(s)$; $\pi(s) \leftarrow \arg\max_{a'} Q(s, a')$, keeping $a$ if it ties for the maximum; if $\pi(s) \ne a$, stable ← false. If stable, stop and return $Q \approx q_*$ and $\pi \approx \pi_*$; otherwise go to 2.
solution: Mirror Figure 4.3, replacing V(s) by Q(s, a).
The improvement step no longer needs p(s′, r|s, a): it compares Q(s, a′) directly.
Keep the current action on ties, the fix for the bug noted under Figure 4.3.
questions.explanation: Model-free control methods (Monte Carlo control, Sarsa, Q-learning) follow exactly this pattern with sampled evaluation.

rubric.point: Initialises Q for every state–action pair and a policy
Evaluation backs up Q(s, a) from Q(s′, π(s′)) with the dynamics, until Δ < θ
Improvement takes argmax over Q(s, ·) directly, without a one-step look-ahead through the model
Handles ties (keeps the current action when it is among the best) so the loop terminates

verification.note: Exercise 4.6, printed p. 110; compared with Figure 4.3, printed p. 97.

questions.stem: Suppose only ε-soft policies are allowed: in every state each action has probability at least $\epsilon / |\mathcal{A}(s)|$. Describe, qualitatively, how steps 3, 2 and 1 of policy iteration (Figure 4.3) would have to change, in that order.
questions.answer: Step 3 (improvement): instead of a deterministic argmax, the new policy is ε-greedy: probability $1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/|\mathcal{A}(s)|$ on a greedy action and $\epsilon/|\mathcal{A}(s)|$ on each other action; the stability test compares these stochastic policies (or just the greedy action). Step 2 (evaluation): the backup must average over the policy's action probabilities, $V(s) \leftarrow \sum_a \pi(a|s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)[r + \gamma V(s')]$, rather than use a single action. Step 1 (initialisation): start from an ε-soft policy (for example the equiprobable random policy) rather than an arbitrary deterministic one. The result is the best ε-soft policy, not $\pi_*$.
solution: Work backwards from what must stay ε-soft: the policy produced by improvement, then what evaluation must handle, then where to start.
questions.explanation: This anticipates on-policy Monte Carlo control with ε-soft policies in Chapter 5.

rubric.point: Step 3: improvement produces an ε-greedy (ε-soft) policy rather than a deterministic greedy one
Step 2: evaluation averages over π(a|s) for all actions
Step 1: initialise with an ε-soft policy; notes the outcome is optimal only among ε-soft policies

questions.stem: In the gambler's problem with $p_h = 0.4$, the optimal policy stakes everything at a capital of 50, but stakes only 1 at 51. Why is such an odd-looking policy a good one?
questions.answer: With $p_h < 0.5$ every flip loses money on average, so the gambler wants to reach $100 in as few flips as possible. At 50 one all-in bet wins with probability 0.4, as good as anything. At 51, staking 49 or more risks dropping below 50 for no benefit; staking 1 instead either reaches 52 or falls back to exactly 50, from which the single bold bet is still available. More generally, small bets near 25, 50 and 75 edge towards these landmark capitals, from which one or two bold bets reach the goal. Many stakes tie for optimal (the draft says the policy is not unique), so the saw-tooth is one member of a family of optimal policies.
solution: Compare the outcomes of stake 1 and stake 49 at capital 51 in terms of the capitals they lead to.
Use v*(50) = 0.4 and the fact that losing small bets returns you to 50.
questions.explanation: Value iteration finds the whole family of tied stakes; the laboratory draws the smallest positive one.

rubric.point: Explains that with p_h < 0.5 fewer flips are better, so bold bets at landmark capitals (50, 25, 75) are optimal
Explains why 51 bets small: a small bet keeps 50 available as a fallback, while a big bet risks dropping below it
Notes that several stakes tie, so the shown policy is one of a family of optimal policies

verification.note: Exercise 4.8, printed p. 111; values recomputed in the laboratory (v*(50) = 0.4).

questions.stem: Write the action-value counterpart of the value iteration backup (4.10): how is $q_{k+1}(s, a)$ computed from $q_k$?
questions.answer: $q_{k+1}(s, a) = \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_k(S_{t+1}, a') \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r|s, a)\big[r + \gamma \max_{a'} q_k(s', a')\big]$, for all $s, a$.
solution: Start from (4.2) and replace q_* by q_k on the right and q_{k+1} on the left.
questions.explanation: This is the full-backup version of Q-learning's update (Chapter 6).

rubric.point: Turns the Bellman optimality equation for q_* (4.2) into an update
Has the max over a′ at the next state, inside the sum over s′, r
Applies to every state–action pair

verification.note: Exercise 4.10, printed p. 111; the iteration is checked to converge to q_* on the 5×5 gridworld.

questions.stem: Why does the draft say classical dynamic programming is of limited direct use in reinforcement learning, though still essential?
options: It needs a perfect model of the environment and a great deal of computation
It only works for deterministic environments
It cannot compute optimal policies, only values
It only applies to episodic tasks
solution: DP assumes a finite MDP known exactly, and sweeps over all states.
questions.explanation: Every later method can be seen as approximating DP with less computation and no perfect model.
optionNotes: Correct: those two assumptions limit it; later methods try to achieve the same effect without them.
DP handles stochastic dynamics through p(s′, r|s, a).
Policy and value iteration compute optimal policies.
DP handles discounted continuing tasks too (e.g. Jack's car rental).

questions.stem: A policy π′ is greedy with respect to $v_\pi$, and in at least one state $q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) > v_\pi(s)$. What does the policy improvement theorem guarantee?
options: v_π′ ≥ v_π in every state, with strict inequality in at least one state
v_π′ > v_π in every state
π′ is optimal
v_π′ ≥ v_π only in the states where the action changed
solution: (4.7) holds everywhere for a greedy π′, so (4.8) holds everywhere; strictness somewhere carries over.
questions.explanation: If no state improves, π was already optimal: v_π satisfies the Bellman optimality equation.
optionNotes: Correct: (4.8) everywhere, strict somewhere.
Improvement can leave some states' values unchanged.
Only an improvement is guaranteed; in Figure 4.2 it happens to be optimal.
The guarantee covers all states, including those whose action did not change.

verification.note: Printed pp. 94–96; checked numerically from random policies.

questions.stem: In a state, two actions tie for the maximum in (4.9) and a third is worse. Which stochastic policies count as greedy improvements in that state? Select all that apply.
options: Probability 1 on the first tied action
Probability 0.5 on each tied action
Probability 0.9 and 0.1 on the two tied actions
Probability 0.45, 0.45 and 0.1 on the three actions
The equiprobable policy over all three actions
solution: Any apportioning among maximising actions is allowed; submaximal actions get zero.
questions.explanation: The bottom-right policy of Figure 4.2 shows such ties as several arrows in one cell.
optionNotes: Correct: any split among maximising actions is allowed.
Correct.
Correct.
The worse action must get zero probability.
Gives the worse action probability 1/3.

questions.stem: True or false: as printed, the policy iteration algorithm of Figure 4.3 may never stop if, at some state, several actions are equally good and the improvement step keeps switching between them.
solution: The draft says so under the figure.
Keeping the current action whenever it ties for best (as our laboratory does) removes the problem.
questions.explanation: The stability test then compares equally good policies and never sees 'no change'.

questions.stem: How does value iteration relate to policy iteration?
options: It is policy iteration with each evaluation stopped after one sweep, the improvement folded into a max
It evaluates every policy exactly, by a linear solve
It improves the policy only once, at the end
It needs a policy as input
solution: (4.10) is (4.5) with the policy's average replaced by a max over actions.
questions.explanation: Between the two lies a whole family of truncated policy iteration methods.
optionNotes: Correct: the max in (4.10) is the only difference from the evaluation backup (4.5).
That is exact policy iteration.
It effectively improves in every sweep; the final greedy policy is only read off at the end.
It needs only the model; the output policy is greedy with respect to the final values.

questions.stem: An asynchronous value iteration backs up one state per step, in an order chosen by the agent's experience. What does it need, with $0 \le \gamma < 1$, to converge to $v_*$?
options: Every state must keep being backed up: each must appear infinitely often
The states must be backed up in a fixed order
Each state must be backed up the same number of times
Nothing: any order converges, even one that stops visiting some states
solution: Asynchronous DP is flexible in order and frequency, but it cannot ignore any state after some point.
questions.explanation: In the undiscounted episodic case some orderings can fail, but they are easy to avoid.
optionNotes: Correct: the order can even be random.
Any order is allowed.
Some states may be backed up far more often than others.
A state that is never backed up again keeps a wrong value.

questions.stem: In generalized policy iteration, suppose both the evaluation process and the improvement process stop changing anything. What can you conclude?
options: The value function and the policy are optimal
Only that the value function is v_π for the current policy
Only that the policy is greedy with respect to some value function
Nothing: GPI need not converge
solution: Stable evaluation: V = v_π. Stable improvement: π greedy with respect to V. Together: v_π satisfies (4.1).
questions.explanation: The two processes compete in the short run and cooperate in the long run.
optionNotes: Correct: the policy is greedy with respect to its own value function, so the Bellman optimality equation holds.
Stable improvement also means the policy is greedy with respect to it.
Stable evaluation also means the values are the policy's own.
If both stabilise, optimality follows.

questions.stem: True or false: in generalized policy iteration, evaluation must run to convergence before each improvement, as in policy iteration.
solution: GPI covers any granularity: value iteration improves after one sweep, asynchronous DP after single states.
questions.explanation: Almost all reinforcement learning methods are GPI with partial, interleaved evaluation and improvement.

questions.stem: What does the draft say about the 'curse of dimensionality' and DP?
options: Large state sets are a difficulty of the problem itself; DP copes with them better than direct search or linear programming
It shows that DP is exponential in the number of states
It makes linear programming the method of choice for large problems
It applies only to continuous state spaces
solution: The exponential growth is in the number of states as variables are added, which any method faces.
questions.explanation: The term is Bellman's (1957).
optionNotes: Correct.
DP is polynomial in the numbers of states and actions; the number of states may grow exponentially with the number of state variables.
Linear programming becomes impractical at much smaller sizes (by a factor of about 100).
It concerns the growth of finite state sets with the number of variables.

questions.stem: Which methods bootstrap, in the draft's sense of updating estimates from other estimates? Select all that apply.
options: Dynamic programming
Temporal-difference learning (Chapter 6)
Monte Carlo methods (Chapter 5)
Averaging complete sample returns for each state

questions.stem: In the bibliographical remarks, the two-array and the in-place versions of iterative policy evaluation are named after classical methods for linear systems. Which pairing is right?
options: Two arrays: Jacobi style (synchronous); in place: Gauss–Seidel style
Two arrays: Gauss–Seidel style; in place: Jacobi style
Both are Newton's method
Two arrays: asynchronous; in place: synchronous
solution: Jacobi: every new value from the old vector. Gauss–Seidel: new values used immediately.
questions.explanation: Both are special cases of asynchronous DP.
optionNotes: Correct.
